Lessons.Title: Shapes and Play
ExplanationParagraphs: First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 7 Lesson 13 source teacher lesson, preparation, original THREE-page student task PDF, park photo and labeled park-plan artwork inspected on the owner PC, plus the original standard square dot paper master. This is a geometry modelling lesson, not a numeric-only worksheet. Source photos and artwork remain publisher-linked and are not embedded. The gated original Cool-down Possible Perimeters has not been reproduced.

Original 3.MD.D.8 objectives: apply geometric attributes, boundary perimeter, and square-unit area to a park design. Teacher phases: warm-up Notice and Wonder: A Park 10 min, Activity 1 Design a Park 20 min, Activity 2 Park Problems 15 min, lesson synthesis 10 min, gated Cool-down 5 min. MLR8 and partner presentations are pedagogical requirements.

Original warm-up page 1 shows an aerial park PHOTO and a distinct coloured A–I labelled path/region diagram of the park. Students notice curved paths, planted regions, and shapes and wonder about the geometry, then discuss how restricting the design to quadrilaterals would change its appearance. There is no unique scalar answer; teacher examines observational claims and discourse.

Original Activity 13.1 page 2: use teacher-supplied square dot paper; ONE horizontal or vertical dot interval equals ONE YARD of real length. Make a small park containing at least FIVE features chosen from basketball court, soccer goal, swings, slide, open area, picnic table, water play area, skate park, or a learner-selected feature. Only horizontal and vertical edges between dots count as 1-yard lengths; diagonal jumps do not equal one yard. For THREE of the chosen features, show numerical AREA in square yards and PERIMETER in linear yards. This is an OPEN visual modelling problem with no single universal key. Teacher must inspect drawn regions, units, feature count and partner explanation.

Original Activity 13.2 page 3 task 1: playground rectangle 6 yards by 14 yards. Fence needed is P=2(6+14)=40 YARDS. Area is A=6×14=84 SQUARE YARDS. Further prompt requests ANOTHER rectangle with the SAME 40-yard perimeter but DIFFERENT area. For example 8 by 12 yields perimeter40 and area96 sq yd, while 10 by 10 yields area100; these are mathematically correct possible answers, not the sole original published solutions. Source allows many dimension pairs; drawing and explanation are teacher-reviewed.

Original Activity 13.2 page 3 task 2: given rectangular open area 48 SQUARE YARDS, find TWO possible perimeter lengths. Feasible examples on the supplied full-grid 19×24 interval sheet are 4 by 12 yards, area48 and perimeter32 yards; 6 by 8 yards, area48 and perimeter28 yards. A 2×24 rectangle would yield perimeter52 yards if drawn with long edge vertically. All have square-area 48; do not confuse the two requested perimeter values with area quantities. No unique ordered answer pair, so allow teacher-graded alternative figures.

Across activities, separate boundary length (yards) from covering area (square yards). Defining park shapes as rectangles can simplify calculations, but students may use other grid-aligned quadrilaterals and composite arrangements if measured correctly. Perimeter may include concave notches. Teacher checks dimensions, whether shapes overlap as represented, and the promised 1 yard per dot interval.

Lesson synthesis asks what partners noticed about SAME AREA rectangles with DIFFERENT perimeters; reversing dimension-pair factor shapes preserves product but changes edge sums. Teacher-led responses and source gated original Cool-down remain separate from new first-party practice. Tests authored, not executed; Stage D, CI, production Rich V2 verification and independent academic approval not claimed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dot paper is yard scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: One horizontal or vertical adjacent-dot interval is one yard.
KeyConcepts.Rule: No diagonal interval counts as one linear yard.

KeyConcepts.Title: Park geometry model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine at least five distinct park features on a source grid.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Describe both P and A for three features.
KeyConcepts.Example: Basketball rectangle 6×14: P40 yd and A84 sq yd.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same perimeter different area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Boundary sum can remain fixed while factor product changes.
KeyConcepts.Example: 8×12 P40 yd and A96 sq yd.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same area different perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Products can match but side sums differ.
KeyConcepts.Rule: ab=48 sq yd and use two different P values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Playground fence and covered area
WorkedExamples.Question: What fence and area for a 6-by-14-yard playground?
WorkedExamples.Check: Source gives two separate items, not interchangeable units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Alternative same perimeter
WorkedExamples.Question: Another 40-yard perimeter rectangle with different area?
WorkedExamples.Answer: 8 by 12 yards is one valid example
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher assesses explanation and constructed figure.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two possible perimeters area48
WorkedExamples.Question: Rectangles with 48 sq yd of area: find two different P lengths.
WorkedExamples.Check: Other mathematically valid perimeter pairs exist.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 84 is square area, not linear boundary.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Report 32 square yards as a perimeter.
Assume one exact park layout/feature sizes.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source is a design challenge with learner-selected features.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks geometric justification, not predetermined scalar shapes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count diagonal dot-to-dot as one yard.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source unit is horizontal/vertical spacing only.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count grid-aligned intervals for exact one-yard edges.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up source photo + A–I aerial schematic are teacher-observed.
Design five of nine source park features; give area and perimeter for any three.
Source park problems 6×14: 40 yards fence and 84 square yards area.
Same perimeter40 can use 8×12 (area96); source area48 can use P28 and P32; alternatives are valid.
Teacher must review model drawings; publisher gated Cool-down and Stage D/CI unverified.
